body.text: Prolific and versatile across various continents, Bruce Beresford, as director and sometimes as producer and writer, has been the great craftsman of Australian film. He was also one of the founders of the new Australian cinema of the 1970s and ’80s, embracing a genre range that included the wild comedy of the Barry McKenzie films (1972, 1974), the subtle coming-of-age drama The Getting of Wisdom (1977), the politically charged drama Don’s Party (1976) and the war and courtroom study Breaker Morant (1980) — and more. And his overseas filmography is similarly diverse, ranging from, say, the Oscar-winning Driving Miss Daisy (1989) to A Good Man in Africa (1994).

Having watched — rewatched — his two latest (and I hope not last) films, Ladies in Black (2018) and The Travellers (2025), I responded as usual to the gift he has shown for the subtle interaction of character and action and for creating a vivid sense of environment in whatever genre. This essay is not intended as a biographical study, so I’ll turn now to these two rewarding films, which I trust will have several successors.

Based on a screenplay by Beresford and his long-time collaborator Sue Milliken, Ladies in Black is adapted from Madeleine St John’s novel, The Women in Black, which Beresford had enjoyed and which had previously been adapted as a stage musical in 2015. The film recalls such earlier Beresford films as The Getting of Wisdom (1977), Puberty Blues (1981) and Paradise Road (1997), not for their genre similarities necessarily, but for what they reveal about how acutely he was able to deal with female protagonists and the settings in which they operate.

Ladies in Black is set in Sydney in 1959, and though there is no sense of biography involved, Beresford did live in Sydney in the 1950s, and the film reflects a persuasive sense of that time and place. There are impressive long-shots of the harbour and its famous bridge and also of the city streets, but the main setting is the vast Goode’s department store (standing in for David Jones), which shines in Peter James’s vivid cinematography. The main visual concern with the eponymous ladies, but there are also enjoyable inserts of their domestic lives.

The central narrative concern with the sixteen-year-old Lisa (Angourie Rice), who is waiting for university entrance but employed over the summer/Christmas period by Goode’s as a temporary assistant to two women in the dress department. These are Fay (Rachael Taylor) and Patty (Alison McGirr), whose personal lives — a new romance for Fay, domestic strife for Patty — get some enjoyable running time. They are friendly towards Lisa, but more influential is Magda (Julia Ormond), an imposing Slovenian émigré who sees real talent in Lisa and takes her on in the Model Gown department.

An element of coming-of-age is now introduced into Lisa’s story. She has aspirations to act and write; and she will graduate from pretty teenager with glasses and girlish hairdo to a more mature-looking young woman, responding to Magda’s firm-minded approach, in a relationship handled without any cliché. Her mother (warmly played by Susie Porter) is very pleased with her success, while her father (Shane Jacobson), reflecting a perhaps typical male attitude in the 1950s, doesn’t want her to go to university.
Throughout, the film melds the personal and professional lives of its protagonists with warmth and understanding of the “ladies in black.”

As to gender matters, the latest Beresford film, The Travellers, is more firmly focused on male characters, though — as in Ladies, where the men are given a share of attention — the women are also able to make their presences felt, even in shorter screentime.

The Travellers opens with a guy arriving at a hotel in Perth (there has been a panoramic shot of the city). He proves to be an opera stage designer called Stephen Seary (played by Luke Bracey) who has returned to Australia from London and is on the way to Yarrabiddy, the small town he grew up in, to see his dying mother in hospital. And, by the way, his background in opera and its later representation in the film recalls Beresford’s own career in opera production, as does his moving between Australia and abroad in the interests of work.

Before visiting his mother he calls at his father’s house, which is in the most chaotic mess, as if Fred, the father (Bryan Brown), has never got rid of anything in his years of living alone. Much of the rest of the film is concerned with relations between Stephen and his grumpy father and his forceful sister Nikki (Susie Porter again), and he also renews acquaintance with a couple of long-ago schoolmates. As written by Beresford, all these characters are sharply delineated, making it easy for the viewer to absorb the shifting relationships and to accept their professions and even Fred’s claim that he “wanted to be an actor.”

This is also a film that conjures with the idea of old age and how those who have reached it have to be dealt with. A doctor tells Stephen’s mother that her condition is largely a matter of age. Stephen tries to talk his father into going to live in “a home,” but Fred insists he can cope — though in one comic episode this is clearly arguable: he is seen showering fully dressed, claiming that, in this way, both body and clothes are getting cleaned. The film deals thoughtfully with the idea of children’s taking responsibility for aged parents.

In a visually effective scene as an estate agent drives Stephen to inspect such a home, the film’s ravishing cinematography captures the beauty of the natural scene not as pictorialism but almost as a recognition of the potential beauty of life at any age. But Peter James’s camera is equally vivid in capturing interiors and contrasting lives, messy or professional, in close-up.

In a cast full of excellent performances, Bracey’s Stephen — always ready for female intimacy as well as getting on with his Traviata-based work — is subtly and sympathetically portrayed. But Bryan Brown’s is perhaps the most stunning performance of his long and prolific career. He imbues Fred with testiness, obstinacy, real feeling — in other words, with life.

And speaking of prolific careers, Beresford’s screenplay and direction suggest that there could be years of quality production still to come. The Travellers has warmth and subtlety along with touches of wit and moments of poignancy, offering a rewarding study of family relations and offering visual and vocal delights along the way.

“Prolific” may always sound impressive and so it is for Beresford, with his capacity to explore lives in their different environments, his fascinating dealings with genre diversity, and his skilful craft, on display in these latest two films in which character, events and ideas collaborate to make for thoughtful entertainment for the observant viewer. •
